# Required Data Structure

Working with the `NEPSroutines` package requires a specific data
structure. This will be explained in the following section. How to
transform the raw data into the required data structure and which
functions of the `NEPSroutines` package may be helpful in this process
is described in Chapter 4 *Data Preparation*.

The package is mainly based on the two datasets `resp` and `vars`. The
**`bold` marked** variable names must be retained as specified. In all
other cases, variable names can be freely chosen.

## Groupings

Sometimes parts of the scaling procedure are conducted separately for
different groups, e.g. different test versions, settings, measurement
occasions, or cohorts. The terms *group* and *grouping* refer to such
cases. However, the functions of the package can only handle one
grouping at a time. If multiple groupings are present (e.g. different
test booklets *and* different cohorts), there are two possible
approaches:

-   On the one hand, analyses can be conducted separately. Since the
    functions of the package can handle at least one grouping, it is
    sufficient to run the analyses separately for the groups of the
    second grouping (e.g. once for cohort A and once for cohort B). The
    first grouping (in our case test booklet version) can then be
    handled normally within the functions. In this case, remember to
    assign a group name using the function argument `name_group`, so
    that results are saved under different names and can be clearly
    assigned to the respective groups (cohort A, cohort B).

-   On the other hand, a grouping variable can be created that contains
    *all* possible combinations of groupings. This can then be used as a
    standard grouping variable in the functions. For two groupings with
    two levels each (e.g. cohorts A and B, test booklets A and B), a new
    grouping variable with four categories would need to be created:

    -   Group 1 for cohort A & test booklet A

    -   Group 2 for cohort A & test booklet B

    -   Group 3 for cohort B & test booklet A

    -   Group 4 for cohort B & test booklet B

## Dataset `resp`

This dataset (`data.frame`) contains all competence items — both scored
and unscored — as well as all information about the test participants,
e.g. sociodemographic variables. Information about each participant is
stored in a single row. An example of this dataset can be seen below for
study B129. The following variables are particularly required:

<table style="width:99%;">
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 73%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th><p>Variable</p></th>
<th><p>Explanation</p></th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><p><strong><code>ID_t</code></strong></p></td>
<td><p>A variable that contains the IDs of the persons.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p>All sociodemographic and methodological variables available per
test person</p></td>
<td><ul>
<li><p>The variables must be numeric. All variables used in the DIF
analyses must be dichotomous in {0, 1}. Non-inherently dichotomous
variables can be dichotomized, e.g. categorizing number of books at home
into &gt; 100 books and &lt; 100 books. Variables used only for
descriptive analyses, e.g. age in schoolchildren, may also be
continuous.</p></li>
<li><p>Missing values are defined as NA</p></li>
<li><p>For an overview of all variables required for scaling, see
vignette <code>preparations</code>.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p>All unscored, scored, and aggregated competence items</p></td>
<td><ul>
<li><p>All unscored items may be numeric, character, or factor
variables.</p></li>
<li><p>All scored items must be integers. Either dichotomous in {0, 1}
or, for polytomous items with k categories, in {0, 1, ...,
k-1}.</p></li>
<li><p>Missing values are coded using negative integers that distinguish
between cases, e.g. -91 = test aborted, -55 = not administered. These
values are referred to as <em>user-defined missing values</em> and
should already be present in the raw data.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p>Additional variables that identify specific persons in the
dataset</p></td>
<td><ul>
<li><p><strong>Validity variable</strong> e.g. <code>valid</code>:
Identifies those persons who have reached a minimum number of valid
responses to be included in the analyses. In our scaling procedures,
this is typically <em>three</em> valid responses.</p>
<ul>
<li><p>The variable must be logical.</p></li>
<li><p>TRUE for all persons with the minimum number of valid
responses</p></li>
</ul></li>
<li><p><strong>Group and grouping variables</strong>, if one or more
groupings are present</p>
<ul>
<li><p>For each grouping, a numeric or factor variable must be created
that assigns each person to a group e.g. <code>difficulty</code>, with
<code>0=easy</code> &amp; <code>1=difficult</code></p></li>
<li><p>In addition, a logical variable must be created per group e.g.
<code>easy</code> <em>and</em> <code>difficult</code> that identifies
all persons belonging to that group</p></li>
<li><p>If items were administered to both groups, an IRT analysis is
usually also performed for all common items. For this purpose, a
variable must be defined in <code>resp</code> e.g. <code>common</code>
that is TRUE for all persons who received the common items — i.e. for
all persons!</p></li>
</ul></li>
<li><p>In individual cases, additional variables may be
required</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

Example for `resp` (from study B129, only the first variables are
shown):

| Variable | Explanation |
|-----------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| **`ID_t`** | Contains the IDs of the persons |
| `sex`, `migration` and `books` | Dichotomous (or dichotomized) sociodemographic variables for descriptive and DIF analyses |
| `difficulty` | Grouping variable assigning persons to the different test booklets |
| `easy` and `difficult` | Group variables identifying persons who received the easy or difficult test form |
| `valid` | Validity variable identifying all persons who have provided at least three valid responses |
| `reg70110_sc2g7` | Unscored simple item with user-defined missing values |
| `reg70131_sc2g7`, `reg70132_sc2g7`, `reg70133_sc2g7` | Unscored sub-items of a polytomous item with user-defined missing values |
| `r eg70110_sc2g7_c` | The dichotomously scored item belonging to `reg70110_sc2g7` (recognizable by the suffix `_c`) with user-defined missing values |
| `r eg7013s_sc2g7_c` | The polytomously scored item belonging to the sub-items (recognizable by the `s` at the end of the item stem and the `_c` suffix) with user-defined missing values |

## Dataset `vars`

This dataset (`data.frame`) contains all information about the
competence items, e.g. item positions, assignment to a test booklet, and
item type. Each version of a competence item (e.g. scored and unscored)
is stored in a separate row (for an overview of the different item
types, see Section 1.1.2 *Competence items*). An example of the `vars`
dataset can be seen below for study B129. How the variables are
constructed is described in Chapter 4 *Data Preparation*. The following
variables are particularly required:

<table style="width:100%;">
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 20%" />
<col style="width: 78%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th><p>Variable</p></th>
<th><p>Explanation</p></th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><p><strong><code>item</code></strong></p></td>
<td><p>A variable containing the item name</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p><code>correct_response</code></p></td>
<td><p>A variable containing the correct answer of the respective item
e.g. 3 if the third response option is correct. Can be a character or
numeric vector.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p><code>type</code></p></td>
<td><p>Variable defining the item type MC, CMC, etc.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p>Position variables</p></td>
<td><p>Indicate the position of the item in the test booklet</p>
<ul>
<li><p>If there are multiple groups, one position variable per group,
even if the position is identical across groups</p></li>
<li><p>Otherwise only one position variable</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p>Logical variables identifying specific items</p></td>
<td><ul>
<li><p><code>raw</code>: TRUE for all <em>unscored</em> items raw
data</p></li>
<li><p><code>distan</code>: TRUE for all <em>unscored</em>
<em>multiple-choice</em> items required for distractor analysis</p></li>
<li><p><code>dich</code>: TRUE for all <em>dichotomously scored</em>
items used e.g. for IRT and DIF analyses. This also includes sub-items
of polytomous items!</p></li>
<li><p>If the item set also includes polytomous items:</p>
<ul>
<li><p><code>poly</code>: TRUE for all <em>polytom scored</em> items
used for data preparation</p></li>
<li><p><code>final</code>: TRUE for all items to be used in scaling used
e.g. for IRT and DIF analyses. This initially includes all
<em>dichotomously scored</em> items <em>excluding</em> sub-items of
polytomous items and all <em>polytomously scored</em> items if an item
was collapsed, then the version with collapsed response
categories.</p></li>
</ul></li>
<li><p>If the item set changes during scaling e.g. because items are
excluded, new variables must be created e.g. <code>dich_new</code> or
<code>final_new</code> that replace the variables above for the new item
set required for all analyses.</p></li>
<li><p><code>suf</code>: TRUE for all <em>scored</em> items without
collapsed response categories that are actually used in the test used
for computation of sum scores, metacognition scores, and creation of the
SUF.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p>Depending on scaling additional variables</p></td>
<td><ul>
<li><p><strong>Grouping variables</strong>, if not all items are
administered in every group e.g. different test booklet versions usually
contain different item sets</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Group variables are always logical variables</p></li>
<li><p>One variable per group e.g. <code>easy</code> and
<code>difficult</code> for easy and difficult test forms</p></li>
<li><p>If items are administered to all groups, an additional variable
e.g. <code>common</code> must be created identifying these
items</p></li>
<li><p>For each grouping variable e.g. <code>easy</code>,
<code>difficult</code> &amp; <code>common</code> and analysis variable
e.g. <code>dich</code>, <code>final</code> &amp; <code>suf</code>, a new
group-specific analysis variable must be created e.g.
<code>dich_easy</code> identifying all dichotomous items of the easy
test form.</p></li>
</ul></li>
<li><p><strong>Scoring variables</strong>, if polytomous items are
included e.g. <code>scoring</code>. These are needed for PCM and GPCM
estimation. The scoring defines how strongly an item contributes to the
analysis. By default, this is 0.5 for polytomous items and 1 for
dichotomous items, but deviations are possible in individual
cases.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Dimensionality variables</strong>, if the test structure
may violate unidimensionality e.g. reading tests with multiple task
groups.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Linking variables</strong>, if linking is performed after
scaling. The required variables depend on the type of linking and data.
See Survey Paper No. 1 Fischer et al., 2016; link above.</p></li>
<li><p>In individual cases, additional variables may be
required</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

An example of `vars` (from study B129, only the first variables are
shown):

| Argument | Explanation |
|-----------------|------------------------------------------------------|
| `item` | Contains the item names |
| `type` and `correct_response` | Variables defining item type and correct response |
| `raw`, `dich` and `poly` | Logical variables identifying unscored, dichotomously scored, and polytomously scored items |
| `distan` | Logical variable identifying all items required for distractor analysis (unscored multiple-choice items) |
| `final` | Logical variable identifying all items included in IRT analyses. Includes all inherently dichotomous items and all polytomous items. If items are excluded or collapsed during scaling, this variable may be updated or replaced (e.g. `final_new`) |
| `easy`, `difficult` and `common` | Logical group variables identifying items belonging to the easy, difficult, or both test versions |
| `suf` | Logical variable identifying items used for score computation and included in the SUF |
| `text_type` and `kog_type` | Variables for dimensionality analyses |
| `scoring` | Scoring variable required for PCM and GPCM |
| `position_easy` and `position_diff` | Position variables specifying item position separately for both test booklets |
| `dich_easy`, `dich_difficult`, `dich_common` | Logical variables identifying dichotomously scored items from the easy, difficult, or both test versions |
| `final_easy`, `final_difficult`, `final_common` | Logical variables identifying polytomously scored and inherently dichotomous items from the different test versions |
| `suf_easy` and `suf_difficult` | Logical variables identifying items used for score computation and SUF creation for each test version |

# Package Structure

The package is strongly oriented toward the scaling of NEPS competence
tests and includes functions for the following parts of the scaling
process:

-   Data preparation

-   Descriptive analyses

-   Analysis of missing values (per person & per item)

-   IRT analyses

-   DIF analyses

-   Distractor analysis

-   Dimensionality analysis

-   Linking

-   Score computation

-   SUF creation

In addition, the package contains general functions that may be useful
for scaling outside the predefined framework. With the exception of data
preparation and descriptive analyses, there is a single **overarching
function** for each scaling section that automatically performs all
necessary calculations and outputs results as plots, tables, and
messages. However, there are also **subordinate functions** that allow
individual steps of each section to be performed separately, enabling
users to refine the original analyses or adapt them to specific needs.
In this guide, the overarching functions are presented in detail, while
the subordinate functions are briefly described.

## Function Output

The output of the overarching functions usually consists of optionally
generated summary results as an Excel table (function argument
`save=TRUE`), the original results in RDS format (function argument
`save=TRUE`), and additional information printed to the console
(function argument `print=TRUE`). Depending on the function, plots may
also be generated (function argument `plots=TRUE`). The tables are
typically designed so that they can be used directly for reporting. The
original results are usually stored as a list containing the unmodified
output of the underlying functions (e.g. TAM functions). These results
can also be printed directly in R (function argument `return=TRUE`). If
they are stored in an R object (by assigning them a name), they can be
further processed directly. For example:

```{r}
irt_results <- irt_analysis()
```

For subordinate functions that perform analyses, a list of results is
always returned. This output, or parts of it, is usually required for
subsequent functions (e.g. for generating plots or result tables). It is
therefore recommended to store the output in an R object (see above).
When using downstream functions, pay close attention to the instructions
in this guide and in the help files (see vignette `general_information`)
regarding which output or which part of the output is actually required!
For subordinate functions that generate plots or tables from results,
users can choose whether these files should be saved (function argument
`save=TRUE`).

# Common Function Arguments

The functions in the package are partially structured in a very similar
way, so that many function arguments are repeated. The most common
arguments are presented in this section, but are not explained in
further detail in the remainder of the guide.

**Input** arguments:

<col style="width: 12%" />
<col style="width: 10%" />

<col style="width: 11%" />
</colgroup>

<th><p>Argument</p></th>
<th><p>Type</p></th>
<th><p>Description</p></th>
<th><p>Default</p></th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><p><code>resp</code> and <code>vars</code></p></td>
<td><p>data frame</p></td>
<td><p>These function arguments require the data frames
<code>resp</code> and <code>vars</code> introduced in the previous
section. They can be passed as they are and do not need to be modified
further.</p></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p><code>select</code></p></td>
<td><p>string</p></td>
<td><p>The analyses are almost always based on only a subset of the
available items or only a specific version of the items. This function
argument requires the name of the logical variable in <code>vars</code>
that identifies the variables required for this analysis e.g.
<code>dich</code> for only dichotomous items or <code>scaling</code> for
dichotomous <em>and</em> polytomous items.</p></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p><code>valid</code></p></td>
<td><p>string</p></td>
<td><p>Optional in most functions. This function argument requires the
name of the logical variable in <code>resp</code> that identifies all
valid cases see section <em>Valid Cases</em> in vignette
<code>data_preparation</code>.</p></td>
<td><p>all cases are used</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p><code>mvs</code></p></td>
<td><p>named <br />
character vector</p></td>
<td><p>Optional in most functions exception: missing value analysis.
Requires a named character vector containing all user-defined missing
values see section <em>User-Defined Missing Values</em> in vignette
<code>data_preparation</code>. Warning: If this vector is incomplete,
severe problems and errors in scaling may occur!</p></td>
<td><p>-999 to -1</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p><code>grouping</code></p></td>
<td><p>character vector</p></td>
<td><p>Optional in some functions. Sometimes parts of the scaling must
be conducted separately for different groups e.g. different test booklet
versions. In this case, this function argument requires a character
vector with the names of the logical variables in <code>resp</code> and
<code>vars</code> that identify all persons or items belonging to a
group. One name is specified per group. Variable names must match
between <code>resp</code> and <code>vars</code> e.g. the variable
<code>easy</code> in <code>vars</code> identifies all items administered
in the easy test version, and the variable <code>easy</code> in
<code>resp</code> identifies all persons who completed the easy test
version.</p></td>
<td><p>NULL</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

**Process** arguments:

| Argument | Type | Description | Default |
|----------|--------|--------------------------------------------|-----------|
| `digits` | integer | Number of decimal places to which the results should be rounded. | usually `3` |
| `warn` | logical | Whether warnings should be printed to the console. | usually `TRUE` |
| `verbose` | logical | Whether the processing steps should be printed to the console. | usually `TRUE` |

**Output** arguments:

| Argument | Type | Description | Default |
|-----------|-------|--------------------------------------------|----------|
| `plots` | logical | In overarching functions, users can choose whether plots of the analyses (e.g. ICC plots and Wright maps in IRT analyses) should be generated. | usually `FALSE` |
| `print` | logical | In overarching functions, users can choose whether (additional) results should be printed to the console or included in the HTML document. | usually `TRUE` |
| `save` | logical | In almost all functions, users can choose whether results should be saved (as `Excel` and/or `RDS`). | usually `TRUE` |
| `return` | logical | In overarching functions, users can choose whether results should be returned in R (as `Rdata`). | usually `FALSE` |
| `path` | string | Path where results should be stored. If the specified folder does not exist, it will be created automatically. In overarching functions, this is split into `path_results`, `path_plots`, and `path_table`. | `"Results"`, `"Plots",` `"Tables"` |
| `overwrite` | logical | Whether Excel tables should be overwritten if they already exist. | `FALSE` |
| `name_group` | string | Name of the *group* to which the analyses refer (e.g. "easy", see 3.1.1 *Groupings*), used to label results, tables, and figures accordingly. Do not confuse this with `name_grouping` (= name of the *grouping*, e.g. "test version") in `mv_person` and `mv_item`! | `NULL` |

In some functions, additional specific arguments are included. These are
described in this guide and can also be accessed at any time via the R
documentation (using the helper functions, see vignette
`general_information`).

# Helper Functions

If parts of the scaling process are carried out without the
corresponding package functions, some of the following functions may be
helpful.

| Function | Usage |
|-------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|
| `convert_mv` | Converts user-defined missing values into NAs. Input arguments are `resp`, `items`, and `mvs`. The output is `resp` with converted missing values. |
| `prepare_resp` | Prepares `resp` for subsequent analyses. Input arguments are `resp`, `vars`, `items`, `valid`, `mvs`, the logical `use_only_valid` (whether only valid cases should be used), and the logical `convert` (whether user-defined missing values should be converted to NAs). The output is `resp` containing only the items defined in `items` as variables, optionally restricted to valid cases and with missing values optionally converted to NAs. |
| `check_folder` | Checks whether the folder specified in the path exists and creates it if it does not. |
| `meht` | Performs the Minimum Effect Hypothesis Test. Input arguments are various statistical quantities. |

# Debugging

Since every scaling procedure is slightly different, it is possible that
errors occur when using the NEPSroutines package. However, in many
cases, the cause of error messages is simply issues in the data
themselves. If a function produces an error message, first check whether
your data are correct: Are all item properties in the `vars` dataset
correctly defined? Does every item in `vars` also appear in `resp` and
vice versa? Do the variable classes match the required specifications?
Have the variables been named correctly? The required data structure is
described in detail in the section *Required Data Structure* and can be
partially checked using dedicated functions (see vignette
`data_preparation`).

If the data are correct and the error still occurs, you can contact
scaling\@lifbi.de with the error message, your script, and the data.
